svg.title: From student pilot to the practical test
svg.desc: Seven steps: choose an aircraft type, get a medical certificate, get a Student Pilot Certificate (age 16, or 14 for glider or balloon), train with a CFI, fly solo with a logbook endorsement, pass the computer knowledge test, then the practical test given by an ASI or DPE. The applicant brings Form 8710-1, the knowledge test report, medical, student certificate, logbook endorsements and the aircraft documents.
svg.text: From student pilot to the practical test
The path PHAK Chapter 1 lays out, in order. The CFI is the one who decides when the student is ready
for each test.
Choose a type of aircraft
Airplanes, gyroplanes, weight-shift, helicopters, powered parachutes, gliders, balloons or airships;
the FAA rules differ by type. No certificate is needed to fly ultralight vehicles.
Get a medical certificate (airplane, helicopter, gyroplane, airship)
Passed with an FAA-authorized AME; the FAA suggests getting it before training starts. Sport pilots
may use a driver license. Balloon and glider pilots write a no-defect statement.
Student Pilot Certificate
Applicant is at least 16 (14 for glider or balloon) and reads, speaks, writes and understands
English. Processed by an FAA inspector or technician, a DPE, a CFI or an ACR; sent in through IACRA.
A plastic card with no expiration date; only needed to exercise solo privileges.
Ground and flight training
Knowledge from FAA handbooks, textbooks and other sources. Each maneuver has four steps: the CFI
demonstrates it, talks the student through it, the student practices under supervision, then the CFI
authorizes solo practice.
Solo flight
A CFI endorses the student logbook for limited solo flight in a specific make and model. No
passengers, no flight in furtherance of a business, and nothing outside the endorsements.
Knowledge test
Computer-based, objective multiple choice. The FAA recommends taking it after a solo cross-country
flight, and the CFI decides when the student is ready.
Practical test (PTS, moving to ACS)
After proficiency and the required hours, the CFI endorses the logbook for the knowledge and
practical tests. Given by an FAA ASI or a DPE; a DPE may charge a reasonable fee, an FAA inspector
does not. All tasks in the areas of operation must be shown, from preflight preparation to
postflight procedures.
Applicant brings
FAA Form 8710-1 (8710.11 for sport pilot) with
the instructor recommendation
Airman Knowledge Test Report with a satisfactory
grade
Medical certificate (not for glider or balloon),
Student Pilot Certificate, and logbook endorsed
for solo, solo cross-country and the make and
model
Graduation certificate from an FAA-approved
school, if applicable
And for the aircraft
An airworthy aircraft with equipment for the test
Registration certificate and airworthiness
certificate
Operating limitations or approved flight manual
Equipment list, weight and balance data,
maintenance records and applicable ADs
